claim: sox1a is expressed in the parapineal from the onset of its formation between 26 and 28 hpf
source: Whole mount in situ hybridisation analysis showed that sox1a is expressed in the parapineal from the onset of its formation between 26 and 28 hpf (Figure 1A–D") (Clanton et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1 and cited reference

claim: sox1a is first expressed in a few cells located on the left side of the forming parapineal at 28 hpf
source: Fluorescent in situ labelling of sox1a mRNA in embryos expressing the Tg(foxD3:GFP)zf104 and Tg(flh:eGFP)U711 transgenes in the whole pineal complex (Concha et al., 2003) revealed that sox1a is first expressed in a few cells located on the left side of the forming parapineal at 28 hpf, and thereafter in all parapineal cells as they undergo collective migration to the left side of the epithalamus (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and cited reference

claim: sox1a is expressed in all parapineal cells as they undergo collective migration to the left side of the epithalamus
source: Fluorescent in situ labelling of sox1a mRNA in embryos expressing the Tg(foxD3:GFP)zf104 and Tg(flh:eGFP)U711 transgenes in the whole pineal complex (Concha et al., 2003) revealed that sox1a is first expressed in a few cells located on the left side of the forming parapineal at 28 hpf, and thereafter in all parapineal cells as they undergo collective migration to the left side of the epithalamus (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and cited reference

claim: sox1a is expressed in the lens vesicle, anterior forebrain, ventral diencephalon, hindbrain and pharyngeal arches
source: Additionally, sox1a is expressed in other areas such as the lens vesicle, anterior forebrain, ventral diencephalon, hindbrain and pharyngeal arches (Figure 1A–D'), as has also been described previously (Gerber et al., 2019; Okuda et al., 2006; Thisse and Thisse, 2004).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1 and multiple cited references

claim: The parapineal migrated with normal timing and trajectory in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Taking advantage of the Tg(foxD3:GFP)zf104 and Tg(flh:eGFP)U711 transgenes to track parapineal cells, we observed that the parapineal migrated with normal timing and trajectory in sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2A-B

claim: Parapineal-specific expression of otx5 was not affected in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Furthermore, parapineal-specific expression of the transcription factor encoding genes otx5 (Gamse et al., 2002) and gfi1ab (Dufourcq et al., 2004) was not affected in the sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C-D and cited references

claim: Parapineal-specific expression of gfi1ab was not affected in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Furthermore, parapineal-specific expression of the transcription factor encoding genes otx5 (Gamse et al., 2002) and gfi1ab (Dufourcq et al., 2004) was not affected in the sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C-D and cited references

claim: Sox1a is not required for parapineal specification
source: These results indicate that Sox1a is neither required for parapineal specification nor for migration.
evidence: Inferred from normal parapineal formation and marker expression in sox1a mutants

claim: Sox1a is not required for parapineal migration
source: These results indicate that Sox1a is neither required for parapineal specification nor for migration.
evidence: Inferred from normal parapineal migration in sox1a mutants

claim: Parapineal efferent projections to the left habenula show reduced outgrowth and branching in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Although parapineal neurons form in sox1a-/- mutants, efferent projections to the left habenula show reduced outgrowth and branching (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2E

claim: By 4 dpf the parapineal projections were either absent or stunted and lacked branching in all sox1a-/- mutant larvae analysed
source: Nevertheless, by 4 dpf the parapineal projections were either absent or stunted and lacked branching in all sox1a-/- mutant larvae analysed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: sox1a-/- mutants have a double-right dHb phenotype
source: Despite normal parapineal specification and migration, sox1a-/- mutants have a double-right dHb phenotype (Figure 3A'–E') compared to wild-type siblings (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and connectivity data shown in Figure 3

claim: The predominantly left-sided expression of kctd12.1 was markedly reduced in all sox1a-/- mutants
source: Hence, the predominantly left-sided expression of kctd12.1 (n = 45) (Gamse et al., 2003) and nrp1a (n = 46) (Kuan et al., 2007a) was markedly reduced in all sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 3A–A' and B–B').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A-A' and cited references

claim: The predominantly left-sided expression of nrp1a was markedly reduced in all sox1a-/- mutants
source: Hence, the predominantly left-sided expression of kctd12.1 (n = 45) (Gamse et al., 2003) and nrp1a (n = 46) (Kuan et al., 2007a) was markedly reduced in all sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 3A–A' and B–B').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B-B' and cited references

claim: There was increased expression of kctd8 in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Conversely, there was increased expression of kctd8 (n = 46) (Gamse et al., 2005) and VAChTb (n = 41) (Hong et al., 2013), which are normally expressed at higher levels in the right dHb (Figure 3C–C' and D–D').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C-C' and cited references

claim: There was increased expression of VAChTb in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Conversely, there was increased expression of kctd8 (n = 46) (Gamse et al., 2005) and VAChTb (n = 41) (Hong et al., 2013), which are normally expressed at higher levels in the right dHb (Figure 3C–C' and D–D').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3D-D' and cited references

claim: The two sox1a mutant alleles (sox1aups8, sox1au5039) failed to complement
source: Similar results were obtained for sox1a morphants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and the two sox1a mutant alleles (sox1aups8, sox1au5039) failed to complement, with trans-heterozygotes for the two alleles showing the same double-right dHb phenotype as sox1aups8 homozygotes (sox1a-/-) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by genetic complementation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: In sox1a-/- mutants, dorsal IPN innervation which normally arises from dHbL neurons was almost completely lost
source: In sox1a-/- mutants, dorsal IPN innervation which normally arises from dHbL neurons (more prominent on the left) was almost completely lost and both dHb projected predominantly to the ventral IPN (n = 15), the target of dHbM neurons (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by anterograde axon tracing data and cited references

claim: Both dHb projected predominantly to the ventral IPN in sox1a-/- mutants
source: In sox1a-/- mutants, dorsal IPN innervation which normally arises from dHbL neurons (more prominent on the left) was almost completely lost and both dHb projected predominantly to the ventral IPN (n = 15), the target of dHbM neurons (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by anterograde axon tracing data and cited references

claim: In sox1a-/- mutants, most left dHb neurons have adopted dHbM character similar to the right dHb
source: This indicates that in sox1a-/- mutants, most left dHb neurons have adopted dHbM character similar to the right dHb.
evidence: Inferred from the projection pattern to ventral IPN

claim: Loss of function of the transcription factor Sox1a leads to double-right dHb phenotype similar to parapineal-ablated larvae
source: In summary, loss of function of the transcription factor Sox1a leads to double-right dHb phenotype similar to parapineal-ablated larvae, despite normal parapineal formation in the mutants.
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple experiments comparing sox1a mutants to parapineal ablations

claim: Transplanted wild-type parapineal cells induced left dHb characteristics in the adjacent (left or right) habenula of sox1a-/- mutants
source: By four dpf, transplanted wild-type parapineal cells induced left dHb characteristics in the adjacent (left or right) habenula of sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 4A'–B' and D'-E'; n = 11), whereas embryos with pineal-cell transplants still exhibited a double-right dHb phenotype (Figure 4C' and F'; n = 5).
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Embryos with pineal-cell transplants still exhibited a double-right dHb phenotype
source: By four dpf, transplanted wild-type parapineal cells induced left dHb characteristics in the adjacent (left or right) habenula of sox1a-/- mutants (Figure 4A'–B' and D'-E'; n = 11), whereas embryos with pineal-cell transplants still exhibited a double-right dHb phenotype (Figure 4C' and F'; n = 5).
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: As few as two parapineal cells were sufficient to change the laterality of the adjacent right dHb
source: As expected, transplanted parapineal cells were also able to induce left dHb characteristics in wild-type right habenula, with as few as two parapineal cells being sufficient to change the laterality of the adjacent right dHb (n = 2; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by transplantation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: sox1a-/- habenulae are competent to respond to the presence of wild-type parapineal cells and adopt left-type character
source: To conclude, sox1a-/- habenulae are competent to respond to the presence of wild-type parapineal cells and adopt left-type character, confirming that the sox1a-/- double-right habenular phenotype results from impaired signalling between the parapineal and the left dHb.
evidence: Inferred from successful rescue of habenular asymmetry by wild-type parapineal transplants

claim: The sox1a-/- double-right habenular phenotype results from impaired signalling between the parapineal and the left dHb
source: To conclude, sox1a-/- habenulae are competent to respond to the presence of wild-type parapineal cells and adopt left-type character, confirming that the sox1a-/- double-right habenular phenotype results from impaired signalling between the parapineal and the left dHb.
evidence: Inferred from successful rescue of habenular asymmetry by wild-type parapineal transplants

claim: Both left and right habenula are competent to acquire left dHb character in response to parapineal signals
source: Furthermore, both left and right habenula are competent to acquire left dHb character in response to parapineal signals, demonstrating that it is the left-sided migration of the parapineal that underlies asymmetric development of the zebrafish epithalamus.
evidence: Inferred from transplantation experiments showing both habenulae can respond to parapineal signals

claim: It is the left-sided migration of the parapineal that underlies asymmetric development of the zebrafish epithalamus
source: Furthermore, both left and right habenula are competent to acquire left dHb character in response to parapineal signals, demonstrating that it is the left-sided migration of the parapineal that underlies asymmetric development of the zebrafish epithalamus.
evidence: Inferred from transplantation experiments showing both habenulae can respond to parapineal signals

claim: Early parapineal ablations at 30 hpf led to overtly double-right habenula development
source: In line with previous studies (Bianco et al., 2008; Concha et al., 2003; Gamse et al., 2005; Gamse et al., 2003), early ablations at 30 hpf led to overtly double-right habenula development, as was evident for all studied markers (kctd12.1, n = 25; nrp1a, n = 6; VAChTb, n = 11) (Figure 5B,G,L) as well as for efferent projections (n = 3) (Figure 5Q).
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 5 and cited references

claim: Parapineal ablations at 35 hpf and 50 hpf did not obviously affect kctd12.1 expression at 4 dpf
source: In contrast, parapineal ablations at 35 hpf (n = 16) and 50 hpf (n = 15) did not obviously affect kctd12.1 expression at 4 dpf (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: Parapineal ablations at 35 and 50 hpf still led to development of double-right efferent projections to the IPN by 4 dpf
source: Surprisingly, however, parapineal ablations at 35 and 50 hpf still led to development of double-right efferent projections to the IPN by 4 dpf (Figure 5R,S; n = 14 and n = 12, respectively), potentially as a consequence of the reduction in axon guidance receptor nrp1 gene expression in the left dHb upon 35 and 50 hpf parapineal ablations (Figure 5H,I; n = 7 and n = 21, respectively) (Kuan et al., 2007b).
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 5R,S and cited reference

claim: Four dpf VAChTb mRNA expression was affected by 35 hpf and 50 hpf parapineal ablations
source: Furthermore, four dpf VAChTb mRNA expression was also affected by 35 hpf (n = 8) and 50 hpf (n = 11) parapineal ablations (Figure 5M,N), indicating that asymmetric neurotransmitter domains are not correctly established upon late parapineal ablations.
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 5M,N

claim: Asymmetric neurotransmitter domains are not correctly established upon late parapineal ablations
source: Furthermore, four dpf VAChTb mRNA expression was also affected by 35 hpf (n = 8) and 50 hpf (n = 11) parapineal ablations (Figure 5M,N), indicating that asymmetric neurotransmitter domains are not correctly established upon late parapineal ablations.
evidence: Inferred from VAChTb expression changes after late parapineal ablations

claim: Upon parapineal ablations at 3 dpf, all studied habenular asymmetries were of wild-type character at 4 dpf
source: Finally, upon parapineal ablations at 3 dpf, all studied habenular asymmetries were of wild-type character at 4 dpf (Figure 5E,J,O,T; n = 7, n = 14, n = 15 and n = 6, respectively), consistent with previous data showing that ablation at this stage does not affect lateralised functional properties of habenular neurons (Dreosti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 5 and cited reference

claim: Habenular asymmetries are regulated at several developmental stages by the parapineal
source: These results indicate that habenular asymmetries are regulated at several developmental stages by the parapineal, firstly at the time of left dHb neurogenesis and thereafter at the level of differentiation (axonal outgrowth and neurotransmitter domains).
evidence: Inferred from time-course ablation experiments showing different effects at different stages

claim: The parapineal regulates habenular asymmetries firstly at the time of left dHb neurogenesis
source: These results indicate that habenular asymmetries are regulated at several developmental stages by the parapineal, firstly at the time of left dHb neurogenesis and thereafter at the level of differentiation (axonal outgrowth and neurotransmitter domains).
evidence: Inferred from time-course ablation experiments

claim: The parapineal regulates habenular asymmetries at the level of differentiation (axonal outgrowth and neurotransmitter domains)
source: These results indicate that habenular asymmetries are regulated at several developmental stages by the parapineal, firstly at the time of left dHb neurogenesis and thereafter at the level of differentiation (axonal outgrowth and neurotransmitter domains).
evidence: Inferred from time-course ablation experiments

claim: In control wild-type embryos, significantly more cells were born in the left dHb compared to the right at 32 hpf
source: In control wild-type embryos (n = 22), significantly more cells were born in the left dHb compared to the right at 32 hpf as expected (p<6×10−5, Wilcoxon signed rank test) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: The asymmetry between the left and right dHb was markedly reduced in parapineal-ablated embryos
source: This asymmetry between the left and right dHb was markedly reduced in parapineal-ablated embryos (n = 18, p=0.002, Wilcoxon signed rank test), due to decreased neurogenesis in the left dHb compared to controls (p=0.004, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test), while the right habenula was unaffected (p=0.478, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: Decreased neurogenesis in the left dHb occurred in parapineal-ablated embryos compared to controls
source: This asymmetry between the left and right dHb was markedly reduced in parapineal-ablated embryos (n = 18, p=0.002, Wilcoxon signed rank test), due to decreased neurogenesis in the left dHb compared to controls (p=0.004, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test), while the right habenula was unaffected (p=0.478, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: The right habenula was unaffected by parapineal ablation at 30 hpf
source: This asymmetry between the left and right dHb was markedly reduced in parapineal-ablated embryos (n = 18, p=0.002, Wilcoxon signed rank test), due to decreased neurogenesis in the left dHb compared to controls (p=0.004, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test), while the right habenula was unaffected (p=0.478, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6E

claim: Compared to wild-type siblings, neurogenesis in the left dHb was reduced in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Compared to wild-type siblings, neurogenesis in the left dHb was reduced in sox1a-/- mutants (p=2×10−4, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test), whereas the right habenula was unaffected (p=0.276, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6F

claim: The right habenula was unaffected in sox1a-/- mutants
source: Compared to wild-type siblings, neurogenesis in the left dHb was reduced in sox1a-/- mutants (p=2×10−4, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test), whereas the right habenula was unaffected (p=0.276, Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6F

claim: There was no significant difference in the 32 hpf BrdU labelling between the left and right dHb of sox1a-/- mutants
source: Therefore, there was no significant difference in the 32 hpf BrdU labelling between the left and right dHb of sox1a-/- mutants (p=0.13, Wilcoxon signed rank test), with both habenula being comparable to the right dHb of wild-type siblings (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by BrdU birthdating analysis shown in Figure 6F

claim: The parapineal is required for the early wave of neurogenesis that is more prominent in the left dHb
source: These results demonstrate that the parapineal is required for the early wave of neurogenesis that is more prominent in the left dHb.
evidence: Inferred from BrdU birthdating analysis showing reduced left dHb neurogenesis after parapineal ablation

claim: The residual asymmetry in the number of BrdU-positive cells between the left and right dHb in parapineal-ablated embryos and sox1a-/- mutants most likely results from a Nodal-dependent (and parapineal-independent) influence upon neurogenesis
source: The residual asymmetry in the number of BrdU-positive cells between the left and right dHb in parapineal-ablated embryos and sox1a-/- mutants most likely results from a Nodal-dependent (and parapineal-independent) influence upon neurogenesis (Roussigné et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on data and cited reference

claim: Left-right asymmetries in the zebrafish habenular nuclei are dependent upon the formation of the parapineal
source: Left-right asymmetries in the zebrafish habenular nuclei are dependent upon the formation of the parapineal, a unilateral group of neurons that arise from the medially positioned pineal complex.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding

claim: Both the left and right habenula are competent to adopt left-type molecular character and efferent connectivity upon the presence of only a few parapineal cells
source: In this study, we show that both the left and right habenula are competent to adopt left-type molecular character and efferent connectivity upon the presence of only a few parapineal cells.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding

claim: The ability to impart left-sided character is lost in parapineal cells lacking Sox1a function
source: This ability to impart left-sided character is lost in parapineal cells lacking Sox1a function, despite the normal specification of the parapineal itself.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding

claim: The parapineal influences neurogenesis in the left habenula at early developmental stages
source: Precisely timed laser ablation experiments demonstrate that the parapineal influences neurogenesis in the left habenula at early developmental stages as well as neurotransmitter phenotype and efferent connectivity during subsequent stages of habenular differentiation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding

claim: The parapineal influences neurotransmitter phenotype and efferent connectivity during subsequent stages of habenular differentiation
source: Precisely timed laser ablation experiments demonstrate that the parapineal influences neurogenesis in the left habenula at early developmental stages as well as neurotransmitter phenotype and efferent connectivity during subsequent stages of habenular differentiation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a main finding

claim: Left-right asymmetries are a consistent feature of all vertebrate brains studied, as well as invertebrate nervous systems
source: Although once considered to be a mark of cognitive superiority of the human cortex, it is now clear that left-right asymmetries are a consistent feature of all vertebrate brains studied, as well as invertebrate nervous systems (Alqadah et al., 2018; Concha et al., 2012; Duboc et al., 2015; Frasnelli, 2013; Frasnelli et al., 2012; Rogers, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references

claim: Lateralisation of brain function has many potential advantages, such as sparing energetically expensive brain tissue, decreasing reaction time by avoiding eliciting incompatible responses, providing an advantage in motor learning and facilitating coordinated behaviour in social animals
source: Lateralisation of brain function has many potential advantages, such as sparing energetically expensive brain tissue, decreasing reaction time by avoiding eliciting incompatible responses, providing an advantage in motor learning and facilitating coordinated behaviour in social animals (Concha et al., 2012; Rogers, 2014; Rogers and Andrew, 2013; Vallortigara and Rogers, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references

claim: The epithalamus displays overt left-right asymmetries in structure and function not only in zebrafish but in a large number of vertebrates
source: With respect to CNS lateralisation, the focus has long been on the epithalamus which displays overt left-right asymmetries in structure and function not only in zebrafish but in a large number of vertebrates, albeit the extent and laterality of these asymmetries varies greatly between different groups (Aizawa et al., 2011; Bianco and Wilson, 2009; Concha and Wilson, 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references

claim: The habenula functions as a relay station conveying information from the limbic forebrain and sensory systems to the ventral midbrain
source: The habenula (Hb) is a phylogenetically old brain structure, which functions as a relay station conveying information from the limbic forebrain and sensory systems to the ventral midbrain (Aizawa et al., 2011; Bianco and Wilson, 2009), whereas the pineal has a conserved role in melatonin release and regulation of circadian rhythms (Ekström and Meissl, 2003; Sapède and Cau, 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: The pineal has a conserved role in melatonin release and regulation of circadian rhythms
source: The habenula (Hb) is a phylogenetically old brain structure, which functions as a relay station conveying information from the limbic forebrain and sensory systems to the ventral midbrain (Aizawa et al., 2011; Bianco and Wilson, 2009), whereas the pineal has a conserved role in melatonin release and regulation of circadian rhythms (Ekström and Meissl, 2003; Sapède and Cau, 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: The zebrafish habenulae are divided into dorsal and ventral habenula (dHb, vHb) on both sides, corresponding to mammalian medial and lateral habenula, respectively
source: The zebrafish habenulae are divided into dorsal and ventral habenula (dHb, vHb) on both sides, corresponding to mammalian medial and lateral habenula, respectively (Aizawa et al., 2005; Amo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: No overt asymmetries have been described in the zebrafish vHb
source: No overt asymmetries have been described in the zebrafish vHb, whereas the left and right dHb exhibit overt differences in cytoarchitecture and molecular signature (Concha et al., 2000; Concha et al., 2003; Gamse et al., 2003), as well as afferent and efferent connectivity (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Gamse et al., 2005; Krishnan et al., 2014; Miyasaka et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017) and function (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Dreosti et al., 2014; Facchin et al., 2015; Krishnan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references

claim: The left and right dHb exhibit overt differences in cytoarchitecture and molecular signature
source: No overt asymmetries have been described in the zebrafish vHb, whereas the left and right dHb exhibit overt differences in cytoarchitecture and molecular signature (Concha et al., 2000; Concha et al., 2003; Gamse et al., 2003), as well as afferent and efferent connectivity (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Gamse et al., 2005; Krishnan et al., 2014; Miyasaka et al., 2009; Turner et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017) and function (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Dreosti et al., 2014; Facchin et al., 2015; Krishnan et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references

claim: The lateral subnucleus (dHbL) is larger on the left side and projects mainly to the dorsal interpeduncular nucleus (IPN)
source: The lateral subnucleus (dHbL) is larger on the left side and projects mainly to the dorsal interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), whereas the medial subnucleus (dHbM) is enlarged on the right side and projects exclusively to the ventral IPN (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: The medial subnucleus (dHbM) is enlarged on the right side and projects exclusively to the ventral IPN
source: The lateral subnucleus (dHbL) is larger on the left side and projects mainly to the dorsal interpeduncular nucleus (IPN), whereas the medial subnucleus (dHbM) is enlarged on the right side and projects exclusively to the ventral IPN (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Left-right asymmetries in the zebrafish dHb are translated into laterotopic dorsoventral innervation of the midbrain IPN
source: Therefore, left-right asymmetries in the zebrafish dHb are translated into laterotopic dorsoventral innervation of the midbrain IPN.
evidence: Inferred from the described projection patterns

claim: Comparable organisation appears to be conserved amongst teleost and jawless fish
source: Comparable organisation appears to be conserved amongst teleost and jawless fish (Signore et al., 2009; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2012; Villalón et al., 2012) but is not obvious in mammals (Kuan et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: The left-sided parapineal is essential for the development of most left-right asymmetries in the zebrafish habenulae
source: In addition to its likely photosensory function, the left-sided parapineal is also essential for the development of most left-right asymmetries in the zebrafish habenulae.
evidence: Supported by multiple studies cited in the following sentence

claim: Mutants in which the parapineal is not properly specified exhibit right isomerism (a double-right phenotype)
source: Mutants in which the parapineal is not properly specified (Clanton et al., 2013; Regan et al., 2009; Snelson et al., 2008) or in experimental setups where the parapineal is laser-ablated at early developmental stages (Aizawa et al., 2005; Bianco et al., 2008; Concha et al., 2003; Gamse et al., 2005; Gamse et al., 2003), left dHb characteristics largely fail to develop and the habenulae exhibit right isomerism (a double-right phenotype).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references

claim: Neurogenesis peaks at 32 hpf in the dHbL (more prominent on the left) and at 50 hpf in the dHbM (more prominent on the right)
source: As shown by 5-bromo-2-deoxyuridine (BrdU) birth-date analysis, neurogenesis peaks at 32 hpf in the dHbL (more prominent on the left) and at 50 hpf in the dHbM (more prominent on the right) (Aizawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: The early onset of asymmetric neurogenesis, marked by expression of the neuronal marker cxcr4b specifically in the left dHb, can already be detected at 28 hpf and requires left-sided epithalamic Nodal signalling
source: However, the early onset of asymmetric neurogenesis, marked by expression of the neuronal marker cxcr4b specifically in the left dHb, can already be detected at 28 hpf and requires left-sided epithalamic Nodal signalling (Roussigné et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Left-sided Nodal signalling determines the direction of parapineal migration
source: Around that time, left-sided Nodal signalling also determines the direction of parapineal migration – in the case of absent or bilateral epithalamic Nodal signalling, parapineal migration is randomised and consequently habenular asymmetries are reversed in 50% of the embryos (Aizawa et al., 2005; Concha et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: In the case of absent or bilateral epithalamic Nodal signalling, parapineal migration is randomised and consequently habenular asymmetries are reversed in 50% of the embryos
source: Around that time, left-sided Nodal signalling also determines the direction of parapineal migration – in the case of absent or bilateral epithalamic Nodal signalling, parapineal migration is randomised and consequently habenular asymmetries are reversed in 50% of the embryos (Aizawa et al., 2005; Concha et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Zebrafish sox1a and sox1b have arisen from an ancestral vertebrate Sox1 gene during teleost genome duplication
source: Zebrafish sox1a and sox1b have arisen from an ancestral vertebrate Sox1 gene during teleost genome duplication (Bowles et al., 2000) and show largely overlapping expression at early stages from 21 somites to 25 hours post fertilisation (hpf) in the telencephalon, hypothalamus, eye field, early lateral line and otic vesicle primordia, trigeminal placode, lens and spinal cord interneurons (Gerber et al., 2019; Okuda et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: sox1a-specific expression has been detected in the lateral line primordium at 24 hpf
source: However, sox1a-specific expression has been detected in the lateral line primordium at 24 hpf (Gerber et al., 2019) and in the parapineal from 26 to 28 hpf onwards, but not the pineal anlage from which the parapineal arises (Clanton et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: sox1a is expressed in the parapineal from 26 to 28 hpf onwards, but not the pineal anlage from which the parapineal arises
